newsitem.title: UK: Soldiers unhurt in N. Irish shooting attack.
newsitem.headline: Soldiers unhurt in N. Irish shooting attack.

text.p: Two British soldiers escaped unhurt in a gun attack in troubled Northern Ireland on Friday, police said.
Three shots were fired at their unmarked vehicle at an intersection near Antrim town, north of Belfast, but they drove on without stopping, a police spokesman said.
No group claimed responsibility for the shooting, which added to rising tension in the British province after a wave of Irish Republican Army (IRA) guerrilla attacks against police and soldiers.
A police spokesman said the soldiers were travelling in an unmarked vehicle.
"The two occupants -- both soldiers -- were unhurt and did not stop," the spokesman said. "When they did get out of the vehicle, they saw three strike marks on the side."

Security sources said IRA militants, intensifying a campaign to end British rule and unite the province with the overwhelmingly Roman Catholic Irish republic, have used mortars and grenades in recent attacks. Shootings have been rare.
On Thursday British forces arrested 11 people in Belfast and Lurgan in a counter-insurgency operation. Late on Thursday a small bomb was thrown at a police vehicle in Lurgan but no one was hurt.

And hours before, soldiers found an IRA-type mortar apparently dumped behind houses in the town. Police said that had it been fired at a military vehicle, a likely target, soldiers would have been killed.

Escalating IRA violence has fuelled fears across Northern Ireland's deeply divided Unionist and Nationalist parties that pro-British Loyalist extremists might abandon a ceasefire they called in October 1994.
Loyalists, so-called because of a fierce allegiance to continued British rule, have been blamed for three attacks on Catholic nationalists since December.
Britain says the Loyalist guerrilla commanders have not called off their ceasefire.
Sunday marks the first anniversary of the abandonment of a ceasefire the IRA proclaimed in September 1994.
The province faces a tense time on Saturday when Loyalists say they will hold a march outside a Roman Catholic church in Harryville, near the town of Ballymena in County Antrim.

The church has been the focus of extremist Protestant protest for some four months, with Loyalists complaining that Catholics in a neighbouring town are preventing Protestants from holding a march to celebrate their Britishness.
